## About & Academic Overview

**Johann Bayer Carpintero** is an Associate Professor, Teaching Stream in the [Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences](https://www.utsc.utoronto.ca/physsci/) at the University of Toronto Scarborough. His academic and pedagogical career is dedicated to physics education, analytical classical mechanics, thermal physics, quantum theory, and relativistic astrophysics.

### Academic Positions
- **Associate Professor, Teaching Stream**: University of Toronto Scarborough, Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences (*Present*).
- **Sessional Lecturer**: University of Toronto (*2005 – 2009*).

### Academic Degrees
- **Ph.D. in Astrophysics**: University of Toronto, Canada.
- **M.Sc. in Astrophysics**: University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada.

### Contact & Departmental Location
- **Work Address**: University of Toronto Scarborough, Department of Physical and Environmental Sciences, 1265 Military Trail, Toronto, Ontario, M1C 1A4 (or M4C 1A4), Canada.
- **Central Research Contact**: 27 King's College Circle, Toronto, ON, M5S 1A1, Canada | Tel: 416-978-2011 | Email: [discover.research@utoronto.ca](mailto:discover.research@utoronto.ca).
- **Academic Tags & Availability**: Physical sciences, Theoretical and computational astrophysics, Industry Projects.

## Teaching & Supervision

Professor Bayer has led core foundational and advanced undergraduate lecture courses across the physical sciences curriculum at UTSC:

| Course Code | Course Title | Description & Curricular Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **PHYC54H3** | **Classical Mechanics** | Intermediate analytical mechanics: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, calculus of variations, central force motion, non-inertial reference frames, rigid body rotation, and continuum mechanics. |
| **PHYC56H3** | **Introduction to Quantum Physics / Quantum Mechanics I** | Quantum foundations: wave-particle duality, Schrödinger wave mechanics in one and three dimensions, operators, eigenfunctions, harmonic oscillator, and hydrogenic systems. |
| **PHYB52H3** | **Thermal Physics** | Classical thermodynamics and introductory statistical mechanics: laws of thermodynamics, entropy, thermodynamic potentials, phase transitions, and canonical ensembles. |
| **PHYA10H3** | **Physics I for Physical Sciences** | Introductory calculus-based mechanics: kinematics, dynamics, work-energy theorem, momentum conservation, rotational dynamics, and simple harmonic oscillations. |

## Research Interests & Scholarly Profile

Professor Bayer's research focuses on **theoretical and computational astrophysics**, specifically **gravitational lensing in general relativity**, optical image singularities, and astrophysical mass constraints on multiple-star and planetary systems.

### Skills and Expertise
- **Gravitational Lensing & Micro-lensing**
- **Astronomy & Theoretical Astrophysics**
- **General Relativity & Relativistic Geometry**
- **Special and General Relativity**
- **Physics Education & Pedagogical Innovation**

### Research Metrics (ResearchGate Profile)
- **Publications**: 3 Major Refereed Articles in *General Relativity and Gravitation*
- **Article Reads**: 370+ Reads
- **Citations**: 11+ Citations by leading international general relativists and pure mathematicians

## Scholarly & Creative Works (Publications)

### 1. Erratum: Maximal lensing: Mass constraints on point lens configurations
- **Authors**: Johann Bayer and Charles C. Dyer
- **Journal**: *General Relativity and Gravitation*, Vol. 39, pp. 1413–1418 (March 2009).
- **DOI**: [10.1007/s10714-007-0463-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10714-007-0463-x)
- **Abstract**: We set constraints and an upper bound on the masses required for a configuration of $n$ point lenses to produce the maximum of $5n - 5$ images of a distant source. We show how this result can be used to detect and constrain the mass of planets or brown dwarfs in multiple-star systems.

### 2. Maximal lensing: Mass constraints on point lens configurations
- **Authors**: Johann Bayer and Charles C. Dyer
- **Journal**: *General Relativity and Gravitation*, Vol. 39, No. 9, pp. 1413–1418 (September 2007).
- **Key Findings & Analysis**:
  - Sets rigorous analytical constraints and mathematical bounds on the perturber masses required to realize maximal image topologies ($5n - 5$).
  - **Figure 3.3**: Central mass perturbation of $m = 1/50$ on a symmetric lens configuration.
  - **Figure 3.11 & 3.12**: Maximum mass for maximal lensing as a function of radial coordinate ($r = 1/2$ and $r = 1/10$).
  - **Figure 5.1 & 5.4**: Fraction $f_1$ of the critical lens area under which caustics open, and fraction $f_4$ of deflector mass enabling planet and substellar detection.

### 3. Gravitational lensing and the maximum number of images
- **Authors**: Johann Bayer, Charles C. Dyer, and Dan Giang
- **Journal**: *General Relativity and Gravitation*, Vol. 38, No. 9, pp. 1419–1428 (September 2006).
- **Abstract**: We show that in a configuration of point masses, replacing one of the point deflectors by a spherically symmetric distributed mass only introduces one extra image. This extra image is located inside the radius of the distributed mass added. We extend a fundamental theorem available for a set of $n$ point masses, proving that the maximum number of images produced by distributed deflectors remains strictly bounded.

### Cited by Prominent Mathematicians & Relativists
Professor Bayer's gravitational lensing theorems have been cited in landmark papers on algebraic geometry, rational functions, and gravitational caustics by:
- **Dmitry Khavinson**: University of South Florida (renowned for solving the Rhie conjecture and Khavinson-Swiatek extremal image bounds).
- **Erik Lundberg**: Florida Atlantic University (harmonic polynomials and gravitational lensing topology).
- **Robert Luce**: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL).
- **Arlie O. Petters**: Duke University (pioneer of singularity theory and mathematical gravitational lensing).
